questions.question: How do BrowserRouter, Routes, Route, and Link work together?
questions.title: React Router’s Basic Navigation Flow
questions.direct_answer: `BrowserRouter` connects routing to the browser History API. `Routes` examines its child `Route` definitions and renders the branch that matches the current URL. Each `Route` connects a path pattern to an element. `Link` changes the URL through the router for user-initiated navigation, normally without requesting a whole new document.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether URL context, matching, route elements, and navigation are connected.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing React Router as page loading without distinguishing server requests.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain browser history and the deployment fallback boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `BrowserRouter` supplies browser URL and history context.
`Routes` matches the current location against its route tree.
`Route` maps a path pattern or index position to UI.
`Link` creates user navigation while preserving normal link semantics.
The web server must still serve the app shell for valid direct URLs.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`BrowserRouter` is the top-level declarative router for a browser application. It observes the browser History API, gives descendants the current location, and responds when navigation changes that location. It normally wraps the part of the application that needs routing.

Inside it, `Routes` evaluates a tree of `Route` elements. A route couples a path pattern to a React element. When the URL is `/about`, for example, the route with `path="about"` contributes its element to the matching branch; an index route represents the parent’s default child.

`Link` is used for navigation the user can choose. It renders link semantics and asks the router to update the history entry, so matching UI changes without the full-document reload caused by a plain same-app request. The browser’s back and forward buttons continue to follow the history entries.

A client-side router does not make the server aware of every application route. Opening or refreshing `/about` sends that path to the server first. An SPA deployment must return its app shell for valid client routes while preserving real asset, API, and missing-file behavior.

Together the components form a URL-to-UI pipeline: the browser location enters `BrowserRouter`, `Routes` selects `Route` elements, and `Link` gives users a semantic way to move to another location.

sections.title: Routing is a mapping from browser location to a rendered branch
sections.content: The URL is application state that survives copying, bookmarking, and browser history. Route definitions describe which elements belong to each location. Links change that location through the router, then matching runs again. This keeps navigation and rendered UI aligned instead of hiding page state in unrelated component flags.

sections.title: Client navigation and document requests are different paths
sections.content:
During client navigation, `Link` lets the router update history and render a new match in the existing document. State outside the changing route branch may remain mounted. A plain external link or a document request goes through the browser and server instead, which is correct when the destination is outside the SPA or a new document is required.

Route matching is declarative. Static segments describe fixed paths, index routes provide default children, and nested definitions build a matching branch. A catch-all client route can render application-level not-found UI, but only after the JavaScript application has loaded. It cannot repair a server that refuses the original document request.

`BrowserRouter` uses clean history-based paths, which makes URLs familiar and shareable. That benefit comes with a hosting requirement: the server must know when to serve the SPA entry document. Hash-based routing avoids that specific server rewrite because the fragment is not sent in the HTTP path, but it changes the URL shape and is a deliberate trade-off.

sections.title: A user click becomes a new matched route
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Link click] --> B[router updates browser history]
  B --> C[BrowserRouter publishes location]
  C --> D[Routes matches route tree]
  D --> E[Route branch renders elements]
  F[back or forward] --> C
  G[direct URL request] --> H[web server]
  H -->|app shell| C
```

questions.question: How do nested routes, Outlet, and useParams work in React Router?
questions.title: Nested Routes, Outlet, and URL Parameters
questions.direct_answer: Nested routes make child paths and UI part of a parent route. The parent layout renders an `Outlet` where the matched child element belongs. A segment beginning with `:` captures part of the URL, and `useParams` reads those string parameters inside the matched branch. The application must still validate a parameter before using it as an ID.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether URL hierarchy, layout composition, and parameter validation are clear.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting Outlet or treating a captured string as a verified resource.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace one URL through the parent, child, parameter, and data states.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A child path is normally relative to its parent route path.
The parent layout must render `Outlet` for child UI to appear inside it.
An index child renders at the parent’s exact URL.
`:projectId` creates a dynamic segment available through `useParams`.
Route parameters are URL strings and can still be missing or invalid domain IDs.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Nested routes describe UI that shares a layout and URL prefix. If a `projects` route contains an index child and a `:projectId` child, the router can match `/projects` or `/projects/atlas` while keeping the projects layout as the parent in both cases.

The parent element renders an `Outlet` at the exact position where the matched child should appear. Navigation, headings, or filters can stay in the parent while the index page or selected project changes inside the outlet. Without that outlet, the child may match but has no place in the parent element to render.

A path segment beginning with a colon is dynamic. `:projectId` captures the text in that URL position, and `useParams` exposes it to components in the matched branch. For example, `/projects/atlas` produces the parameter `projectId = "atlas"`.

The parameter is only a string from the URL, not proof that a project exists or that the current user may view it. The component or data layer must validate the format, load the resource, and represent pending, not-found, forbidden, and failure states appropriately.

The mental model is a tree: parent routes contribute shared UI, `Outlet` is the child slot, and parameters carry variable URL data into the selected branch.

sections.title: The route tree becomes both a URL hierarchy and a UI hierarchy
sections.content: Nesting is useful when several screens share chrome or data boundaries. Each matched level contributes an element, and outlets connect those levels. Dynamic segments keep resource identity in the URL so a specific view can be shared, bookmarked, refreshed, and restored by browser history.

sections.title: Match the branch first, then validate the captured value
sections.content:
For `/projects/atlas`, the router matches the `projects` parent and its `:projectId` child. It renders the parent element, then supplies the child element to the parent’s `Outlet`. An index child has no extra segment and renders when the parent URL is matched exactly. A pathless layout can add shared UI nesting without adding a URL segment.

`useParams` returns the captured segment names for the active branch, and child routes inherit parent parameters. Their values reflect URL text, so a numeric ID still begins as a string and must be parsed and checked. A syntactically valid ID may still return no record, which should produce intentional not-found UI rather than a crash or an empty panel.

Relative child paths and relative links make a feature easier to move under a different parent. Absolute paths are useful when navigation truly targets an application-wide location. The route structure should follow stable information architecture rather than every small component boundary; excessive nesting can make loaders, errors, and navigation harder to trace.

sections.title: One URL selects a parent layout and a parameterized child
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[/projects] --> B[ProjectsLayout]
  B --> C[Outlet]
  C -->|exact parent URL| D[index child: project list]
  C -->|/projects/:projectId| E[ProjectPage]
  E --> F[useParams reads projectId]
  F --> G{known and allowed?}
  G -->|Yes| H[render project]
  G -->|No| I[render not-found or forbidden state]
```

questions.question: When should you use Link or NavLink instead of useNavigate?
questions.title: Declarative Links vs Programmatic Navigation
questions.direct_answer: Use `Link` when the user is choosing a destination and `NavLink` when that link also needs active styling; Data and Framework modes can expose pending styling too. They preserve link meaning and browser interactions. Use `useNavigate` when code must move after an event that is not itself a destination link, such as a successful form submission or session timeout.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether navigation tools are chosen by semantic and history intent.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using click handlers for destinations or navigating before an action succeeds.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain link semantics, active navigation, and replace behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `Link` is the default for visible user-chosen destinations.
`NavLink` adds active state; pending state is available in Data and Framework modes.
Links preserve semantics such as open in a new tab and copy address.
`useNavigate` is for event-driven navigation after application logic.
Use `replace` when the previous history entry should not remain a return target.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`Link` and `NavLink` are declarative navigation. They describe a destination in rendered UI, so users, keyboards, assistive technology, and browser link actions can understand it. `NavLink` is useful for menus because its callback state identifies the active destination; Data and Framework routers can also expose a pending destination.

For example, a project name in a list should be a `Link` to that project. A dashboard sidebar can use `NavLink` so the current section has an active class and `aria-current` behavior. Replacing these with click handlers on generic elements would remove useful browser and accessibility semantics.

`useNavigate` is imperative. It is appropriate when navigation is the result of completed logic rather than the primary meaning of a rendered control. After a login request succeeds, code may navigate to the dashboard. A session timeout may navigate to sign-in, and a cancel action may deliberately move to a known return route.

History behavior matters. Pushing a destination keeps the current location for the Back button. Using `replace: true` replaces it, which is often suitable after login or a redirect-like correction. Going by a numeric delta assumes a usable history entry, so a stable destination can be safer for an application-level Back control.

The rule is semantic: if the interface says ‘go there,’ render a link. If application state says ‘the flow has now moved there,’ navigate in code after that state change succeeds.

sections.title: Declarative and programmatic navigation
sections.content: A destination the user can inspect and choose belongs in the document as a link. A transition caused by a completed workflow belongs in event logic. This distinction improves keyboard behavior, discoverability, browser history, testability, and the ability to open destinations in another tab.

sections.title: Navigation carries both destination and history intent
sections.content:
`Link` intercepts eligible in-app navigation while still rendering an anchor-based interaction. Modified clicks and browser conventions remain meaningful. `NavLink` builds on that behavior with active state and, in Data or Framework mode, pending state. Active styling should not rely on color alone; the link also receives `aria-current="page"` when active.

`useNavigate` returns a function that can target a path, optionally replace the current history entry, or move by a history delta. It should run from an event or effect with a genuine state-driven reason. Calling it during render creates a side effect in the wrong phase and can produce unstable behavior.

Data and framework router APIs may offer redirects in actions or loaders, which can express data-driven routing earlier than a component effect. In a declarative component flow, navigating after an awaited submit is still a clear use. Never navigate before the operation has actually succeeded unless the design intentionally uses optimistic behavior and can recover.

sections.title: Match the navigation tool to the interaction
sections.content:
| Situation | Use | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Item opens a detail page | `Link` | The destination is the control’s meaning |
| Sidebar shows current section | `NavLink` | Adds active or pending route state |
| Login request succeeds | `useNavigate` | Navigation follows completed logic |
| Session expires | `useNavigate` with `replace` | Code redirects and avoids returning to protected UI |
| External website | Plain `a` | It is a document navigation outside the router |

sections.title: Use links for choices and navigate after a successful action
